extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (primary) and patent practitioners/applicants (secondary)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether patent claims integrate judicial exceptions (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas) into a practical application under the Alice/Mayo framework. Covers when additional claim elements are merely instructions to apply an exception, insignificant extra-solution activity, and field-of-use limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere Instructions To Apply An Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: When determining whether a claim integrates a judicial exception into a practical application (Step 2A Prong Two) or recites significantly more than a judicial exception (Step 2B), consider whether the additional elements amount to more than a recitation of the words "apply it" (or an equivalent) or are mere instructions to implement an abstract idea or other exception on a computer. The additional element or combination of elements must do "more than simply stat[e] the [judicial exception] while adding the words 'apply it'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court examples (Mayo, Alice, Benson) show recitations that merely instruct application (e.g., measuring metabolites, intermediated settlement on a generic computer, BCD-to-binary conversion) do not render an exception eligible. Examiners may explain on the record why additional elements do or do not meaningfully limit the judicial exception. Consider overlap with other MPEP considerations—improvement, particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional—when making determinations, but do not evaluate the well-understood/routine/conventional consideration in Step 2A Prong Two (that's for Step 2B). See MPEP §2106.07(a) for formulating a subject matter eligibility rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether the claim recites only the idea of a solution or outcome (i.e., fails to recite details of how a solution to a problem is accomplished). Claims that attempt to cover any solution to an identified problem with no restriction on how the result is accomplished and no description of the mechanism are equivalent to the words "apply it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result-oriented claims that lack details about how a computer or other components perform modifications are likely ineligible (e.g., Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One — modifying XML without specific steps held ineligible). In contrast, claiming a particular solution or a particular way to achieve a desired outcome may integrate the exception into a practical application or provide significantly more. Case citations: Electric Power Group v. Alstom; Intellectual Ventures I v. Symantec; Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network; Intellectual Ventures I v. Capital One (examples and precedent discussed). Examiners should analyze whether the claim describes specific steps/mechanisms rather than only an outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the claim invokes computers or other machinery merely as a tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the claim invokes a computer or other machinery merely as a tool to perform an existing process (i.e., using the machine in its ordinary capacity for economic or other tasks) or simply adds a general-purpose computer/components to an abstract idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of machinery in its ordinary capacity (receive, store, transmit data) or claiming improved speed/efficiency solely from applying the abstract idea on a computer does not integrate the exception into a practical application or provide an inventive concept (examples: Affinity Labs v. DirecTV; TLI Communications v. AV Auto; Intellectual Ventures I LLC v. Capital One Bank). By contrast, claims that improve computer capabilities or an existing technology may integrate the exception (examples: McRO; Enfish). Examples of mere-tool use: telephone unit and server used in ordinary capacity to record/administer/archive digital images (TLI). See MPEP §§2106.04(d)(1) and 2106.05(a) for discussions of improvements to computer functioning or other technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: The particularity or generality of the application of the judicial exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the particularity (specific, confined application) versus generality (broad applicability across many fields) of the claimed application of the judicial exception. Broad claims that generically recite an effect or claim every mode of accomplishing that effect may merely be adding the words "apply it."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that generically state results or effects without describing methods of achieving them are less likely to meaningfully limit the exception (e.g., Internet Patents Corp. v. Active Network). Limitations that confine the exception to a particular, practical application (specific configuration/location/features) may amount to significantly more or integrate the exception into a practical application (e.g., BASCOM — installation of filtering tool at a specific remote ISP location with customizable features; DDR Holdings — manipulated Internet interactions that overrode conventional hyperlink behavior). Historical examples include O'Reilly v. Morse and The Telephone Cases (monopolization of a natural force or claiming all means to achieve an effect deemed ineligible). Consider whether the limitation confines the abstract idea to a particular practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant Extra-Solution Activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether additional elements add more than insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception. "Extra-solution activity" consists of activities incidental to the primary process or product that are nominal or tangential additions (includes pre-solution activities such as gathering data and post-solution activities such as outputting results). The addition of insignificant extra-solution activity does not amount to an inventive concept, particularly when the activity is well-understood or conventional.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition and examples: pre-solution activity (gathering data for a claimed process), post-solution activity (printer/output not integrated into claim). Supreme Court and Federal Circuit precedent (Parker v. Flook; Mayo) show post-solution or measuring steps can be insignificant. Examiners should consider other MPEP factors (particular machine/transformation, well-understood/routine/conventional, field of use/technological environment) when determining insignificance, but should not evaluate well-understood/routine/conventional in Step 2A Prong Two (that's Step 2B). When an element adds insignificant extra-solution activity, examiners should explain in the rejection why it does not meaningfully limit the claim (see MPEP §2106.07(a)). Specific considerations examiners may use: (1) Whether the extra-solution limitation is well known (token extra-solution activity); (2) Whether the limitation is significant (imposes meaningful limits on the claim); (3) Whether the limitation amounts to necessary data gathering and outputting (all uses of the recited exception require such gathering/output). Examples of activities found to be insignificant extra-solution activity: Mere data gathering (clinical tests to obtain inputs, testing system responses, presenting offers and gathering statistics, obtaining Internet transaction info to verify credit card transactions, consulting/updating logs, determining biomarker levels); Selecting a particular data source/type (limiting database index to XML tags, taking only certain customer orders, selecting types of information for a power grid display, requiring user request to view an advertisement); Insignificant application (cutting hair after determining style, printing/downloading generated menus). Some cases identify insignificant computer implementation as an example (Fort Properties v. American Master Lease; Bancorp Services v. Sun Life) while others treat such limitations as mere instructions to apply an exception (see MPEP §2106.05(f)). Examiners should give concrete explanations when relying on insignificant extra-solution activity to support an eligibility rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of Use and Technological Environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider whether additional elements do more than generally link the use of a judicial exception to a particular technological environment or field of use. Merely indicating a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception does not amount to significantly more than the exception itself and cannot integrate the exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supreme Court precedent (Diamond v. Diehr; Parker v. Flook) establishes that limiting an abstract idea to a field of use or adding token post-solution components does not make the concept patentable. Use Flook as a classic example: applying a mathematical formula "in a process comprising the catalytic chemical conversion of hydrocarbons" did not render the formula patentable. Examiners should ensure that field-of-use limitations do more than token narrowing and instead materially confine the claim to a practical application if relied upon to show eligibility.
